en: The *Iśvararāja-bodhisattva-sūtra*, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.

At the Jeta Grove, he was together with a great assembly of twenty thousand bhikṣus and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who were all in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha). Their names were:
Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Siṃhamati Bodhisattva, Siṃhavyūha Bodhisattva, and Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva; with these as leaders, there were ten thousand such beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly who paid him respectful homage, as he expounded the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings who had resolved upon the Mahāyāna.

At that moment, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva named Īśvararāja, who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask something; if you would grant me leave, I shall venture to speak.
The Buddha told King Vaśavartin:
"Regarding whatever you may ask, there is nothing the Buddha will not permit. Ask as you wish, and I shall explain it for you so that you may attain understanding."
Having received this permission, the Bodhisattva Vaśavartin was filled with immeasurable joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain sovereign practice within the Mahāyāna Dharma, such that they are able to expound this Dharma for others; and by means of their power of mastery, how do they subdue all Māras, those with overweening pride, and all non-Buddhists who hold views and are attached to acquisitions, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna, fulfill great vows, achieve the practice of precepts, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sovereign King:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Since you are able to ask the Buddha about this matter, I shall explain it for you; listen attentively with a single mind and reflect upon it well.
How can all bodhisattvas cause sentient beings to abide in the Mahāyāna, fulfill their great vows, accomplish the practice of the precepts, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Bodhisattva Sovereign King (Vaiśravaṇa-rāja) received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha told Sovereign King:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four dharmas of mastery; by means of these dharmas, they are able to act with mastery, enabling all sentient beings to abide in the Mahāyāna.”
What are the four?
First, mastery over ethical discipline;
second, mastery over supernormal powers; [and so forth].
Third is mastery over knowledge;
fourth is mastery over wisdom.
Regarding mastery over ethical discipline, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline, neither violating nor failing it.
It is unblemished, untainted, free from attachment, without regret or reproach, free from feverish distress, praised by the wise,
the precept of conformity to the Path, the precept of teaching sentient beings, the precept of protecting the Dharma, the precept of joy,
the precept of non-reliance on place of birth, the precept of abiding in concentration, the precept of conforming to wisdom, and faith.
The precept of understanding profound dharmas; the precept of non-retrogression in supernormal powers; the precept of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the precept of quiescence; the precept of gathering the Buddha-dharmas; the precept of expounding the Buddha-dharmas; the precept of not abandoning any sentient beings;
the precept of compassionate protection; the precept that is the root of great compassion; the precept of pure faith; and the precept of unchanging ritual conduct.
The precepts of the subtle practices of *dhūta*; the precepts of accord with the field of merit; the precepts of ultimate purity; the precepts of not severing the lineage of the Buddha;
the precepts of protecting the lineage of the Dharma; the precepts of manifesting the noble assembly; the precepts of abiding securely in the bodhicitta; the precepts that assist the six *pāramitās*;
the precepts for cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness; and the precepts for cultivating the four right efforts and the four bases of power.
It is the precept that perfects the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
it is the precept that can give rise to all factors conducive to enlightenment. Sovereign King!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can uphold such precepts, their morality will be complete and all their aspirations will be fulfilled.

If a bodhisattva upholds such pure precepts, when the trichiliocosm is consumed by flames at the end of the kalpa, should they wish to extinguish the fire, saying, "The fire shall be extinguished," the fire will immediately be extinguished.

If one wishes to transform the entire trichiliocosm into water; if one wishes to cause a universal rain of various flowers to fall upon the trichiliocosm; if one wishes to cause the trichiliocosm to become entirely composed of precious jewels; if one wishes to merge all the Mount Sumerus of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges into a single mountain; or if one wishes to merge the great oceans of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges into a single ocean—all these are accomplished according to one's will and there is nothing that is not achieved. Because of the power of upholding the precepts, all aspirations are fulfilled, and the supernatural powers exercised never fail to accord with one's intent.

When a bodhisattva is established in such precepts and attains such sovereign power, because they maintain pure morality, their profound vows are fully accomplished, and they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Vasavartin! In the distant past, beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there was a Buddha named Śuddhaprabhāśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.”

At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Vajrānta, who, having attained the power of upholding the precepts and practicing pure morality, constantly practiced walking meditation in secluded forest groves, cultivating right conduct in order to fulfill the Buddha-dharma.
Having cultivated corrective conduct, one forms this thought:
"The non-apprehension of all dharmas is what is called precept;
the absence of craving for all dharmas is what is called precept."
To extinguish all fetters is what is called precept;
to contemplate the body as being like a reflection in a mirror is what is called precept;
to regard all speech and words as being like an echo is what is called precept.
To contemplate the nature of the mind as being like an illusion is called precept;
that wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are neither dual nor distinct is called precept;
and to contemplate the impurity of the body for the sake of overcoming desire is called precept.
To give rise to a mind of loving-kindness because of hatred is called precept;
to shatter the net of delusion with wisdom is called precept;
to not find the root of greed and hatred is called precept.
To have no contemplation and no conceptual discrimination regarding phenomena is what is called precept;
to have no view of a self, no view of a sentient being, no view of a life-span, no view of a person, no view of permanence, and no view of cessation is what is called precept;
to neither produce nor give rise to any phenomenon is what is called precept.
A mind free from fear is what is called precept;
not relying on the three realms is what is called precept;
faith in the dharma of non-arising is what is called precept.
To have faith and resolve in the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is called precept;
not coveting gain or offerings is called precept;
to have a mind that is not startled or terrified by the emptiness of all dharmas, to destroy and depart from all signs, and to eliminate all vows is called precept.
A mind free from conceptualization is what is called precept;
not exalting oneself and not disparaging others is what is called precept;
non-attachment to the sense bases is what is called precept.
Not giving rise to the five desires is what is called precept;
thoroughly understanding that the aggregates are identical to the aggregate of dharmas is what is called precept;
thoroughly understanding that all natures are identical to the nature of dharmas is what is called precept.
To delight in the absence of contention and dispute is what is called precept;
to not abandon diligent practice within the wholesome dharmas is what is called precept;
to know that all dharmas possess the characteristic of ultimate quiescence and to realize this through bodily experience is what is called precept.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
When the bhikṣu Vajrasama was thus established in the precepts, cultivating the noble Dharma with right mindfulness and without error, there was a son of Māra named Obstruction.

Seeing the bhikṣu Vajrasama thus upholding the precepts and cultivating the noble Dharma with right mindfulness and without error, he came to that place accompanied by eighty-four thousand māras and their retinues, donning armor and bearing weapons. Concealing his own body, he observed where the mind of this bhikṣu was directed."
For a thousand years he followed [the practitioner], yet he could not find even a single moment of distracted thought that could be disturbed or destroyed.
Thereupon, the son of Māra and his retinue manifested their demonic forms, brandishing swords and spears, and stood before the bhikṣu, intending to terrify him.
When the bhikṣu saw the great host of Māra’s army with their weapons, intending to terrify him, he made this vow:

"If my precepts are pure, and I have practiced the noble Dharma and right conduct without error, then by virtue of these causes and conditions, may the weapons of Māra’s host all be transformed into lotuses of blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated colors, as well as *sumanā* flowers, *pāriśa* flowers, and other wondrous, famous blossoms, serving as necklaces; and at that time, may the sons of Māra and their retinues, in form, color, and deportment, all become like my own."
"Lord of Sovereignty!

When the bhikṣu Vajrasama spoke these words, the weapons of the hosts of Māra were immediately transformed into flowers of exquisite color, with their sublime, wonderful fragrance and purity serving as necklaces."
All the Māras saw themselves as being like this bhikṣu, with his hair and beard shaven and wearing dyed saffron robes.

When the sons of Māra saw the bhikṣu manifesting such great supernormal power, they marveled at this unprecedented event and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder; together with their retinues, they prostrated at his feet and spoke these words:
"What Dharma have you attained that you possess such power?"
The bhikṣu said:

"This power does not arise from anything that can be apprehended, nor does it arise based on body, speech, mind, or any phenomena. This power does not arise by abiding in signs, because it has no place of abiding."
The Māra said:
"Bhikṣu! For a thousand years I have sought the movements of your mind, yet I cannot find their location."
The bhikṣu said:
"Even if you were to seek it for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, you still could not obtain it. Why is this?"
"This mind is neither within, nor without, nor in between. Can you possibly find the place where the mind of a conjured person acts?
He replied, "A conjured person has no mind at all, much less a place where that mind acts."
The bhikṣu said:
“The Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are empty and like illusions; herein there is neither mind nor volition.
Māra said:
"If one does not find the mind and does not find thought, how can there be coming and going,
or speech? The bhikṣu replied,
"The coming, going, and speaking of an illusory person are just like my own coming, going, and speaking."
The Māra said:
“By means of this practice, you abide in the observance of precepts; toward what goal do you cultivate the noble Dharma?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Proceeding where there is no place to proceed.
Māra asked: "How does one proceed where there is no place to proceed?"
The bhikṣu said:
"In this, there is no one who has gone before, no one who is going now, and no one who will go; there is no destination. This is precisely the gate of liberation through non-action."
Regarding your question:
"By proceeding thus and abiding in the training of the noble Dharma through the precepts, where does one go?"—I do not go toward the arising of form, nor do I go toward the cessation of form;

I do not go toward the abiding of form, nor do I go toward the cessation or the abiding of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), I likewise do not go toward their arising, nor toward their cessation, nor toward their abiding. This is called "right going."
"Son of Māra!

One who is correctly directed is called one who does not grasp at form, nor grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is no dharma perceived as that toward which I am directed.

That toward which I am directed is such that one does not grasp at form, nor grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; that toward which I am directed is that which all the noble ones direct themselves toward."
The Māra said:
“Bhikṣu! Within this Dharma, what is there to be attained?”
The bhikṣu said:
"The dharmas of all ordinary beings and the dharmas of all Buddhas are the same single dharma, without duality or distinction;
the dharmas of those in training, the dharmas of arhats, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of Buddhas are the same all-encompassing dharmas, without duality or distinction."
Whether they be dharmas of the past, dharmas of the future, or dharmas of the present, they are all one and the same dharma, without duality and without distinction;
for they are without emergence or birth, owing to their identical characteristics.

One who does not abandon such equal characteristics of all dharmas preaches the Dharma for the sake of demonstrating these dharmas to sentient beings; one who proceeds in this manner is said to be proceeding correctly.
"O Son of Māra!
One who is truly progressing does not progress toward the realm of desire, does not progress toward the realm of form, and does not progress toward the formless realm.
One who abides in the equality of all phenomena remains unmoved and non-retrogressive regarding the true nature of phenomena; this is called 'true progression.'"
As is the course of suchness, so too is the course of all dharmas;
as is the course of the dharma-nature, so too is the course of all dharmas;
as is the course of the limit of reality, so too is the course of all dharmas.
"One who seeks such a destination does not even think of or cling to any of the realms of existence; this is called the 'right destination.
The son of Māra said to the bhikṣu Vajrasaṃhati, "By means of this right practice, what dharma have you attained?"
He replied:

"By means of this right practice, I have attained detachment from the discrimination of all phenomena; because of this state of non-thought and non-discrimination, I am fully endowed with the mark of equality."
Regarding your question, "What dharma is attained?":

within right practice there is no characteristic of attainment and no overweening pride; because this right practice finds nothing to be attained in dharmas, the meaning of right practice is precisely non-practice.
The son of Māra asked the bhikṣu Vajrasama:
"By means of this precept, what dharma will you attain?
He replied:
"I shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of these precepts, because even the slightest phenomenon is unattainable.
The son of Māra asked:
"How can one attain enlightenment?"
The bhikṣu said:

"Form and so forth are the attainment of bodhi; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and so forth are the attainment of bodhi; all dharmas and so forth are the attainment of bodhi."
The son of Māra asked:
"In what place is such bodhi to be sought?
The bhikṣu replied:
"You should seek it within the very nature of my view.
The son of Māra asked,
"How should one seek it?"
The bhikṣu said:
"When seeking, I do not give rise to the view of bodhi. Māra said:
“Bhikṣu! Who is your teacher?
By whom have you been instructed that your eloquence is such as this?”
The bhikṣu said:
"One who attains bodhi without destroying the nature of my views is my teacher;
one who abides neither in defilement nor in purity is my teacher."
If consciousness abides neither in the conditioned nor in the unconditioned, he is my teacher;
if he has not heard all dharmas from another, yet abides in neither grasping nor abandoning and is able to cross over the floods, he is my teacher;
if he thoroughly knows all dharmas yet does not arrive at any dharma, he is my teacher.
If all spoken sounds and words do not waver within the ineffable nature of all phenomena, he is my teacher;
if all phenomena are unarisen, unproduced, and unemerged, yet he is able to turn the holy wheel of Dharma, he is my teacher;
if he does not abide on this shore, nor on the other shore, nor in the middle stream, he is my teacher.
If all dharmas arise because they do not arise, then he is my teacher;
if all dharmas cease because they do not cease, then he is my teacher.
Following the instruction of such a teacher, I therefore argue in this manner.
The son of Māra asked:
"By what means does the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma?
He replied:
“The Tathāgata does not turn forward nor turn back with respect to form;

the suchness of form, the dharma of form, the emptiness of form, the signlessness of form, the wishlessness of form, the cessation of form, the detachment of form, the non-arising of form, the characteristic of form, and the nature of form likewise do not turn forward nor turn back.

With respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they do not turn forward nor turn back; the suchness of consciousness, the dharma of consciousness, the emptiness of consciousness, the signlessness of consciousness, the wishlessness of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, the detachment of consciousness, the non-arising of consciousness, the characteristic of consciousness, and the nature of consciousness likewise do not turn forward nor turn back.”
Because all dharmas do not revolve, the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma.
Whether this wheel of Dharma revolves or does not revolve, it ultimately never transcends the immeasurable nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
"If one can understand this turning of the wheel of Dharma, that person is able to turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the son of Māra and his retinue all became disciples of the bhikṣu Vajrasama and spoke these words:
"From this day forward, we take refuge in our teacher."
The bhikṣu said:
"Do not take refuge in me; you should take refuge in the Buddha King of Pure Radiant Light. What I have spoken is the teaching of the Buddha."
The son of Māra said, "We may go together to the Buddha.

Then the bhikṣu Vajrasama, together with the son of Māra and an assembly of eighty-four thousand māras, went to the place where the Buddha Pure Radiant Light King was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and stood to one side.

The Buddha King of Pure Radiance, on account of their pure precepts and practice of the noble Dharma, preached such a teaching for them, whereby they all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Vasavartin! Do you think that the bhikṣu Vajrasaṃhati at that time was someone else?
It was none other than yourself."
The son of Māra named Obstructer was the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Earth-Upholder.
Sovereign King!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mastery over ethical discipline.

When a bodhisattva attains this mastery over ethical discipline, they are able to manifest inconceivable power of vows to sentient beings, teaching and transforming immeasurable beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, they are able to personally subdue the maras and their adversaries, swiftly achieving *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha told Sovereign King:
"What is meant by the sovereign mastery of the supernatural powers (abhijñā) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
It refers to the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, and the bases of psychic power."
"Lord of Sovereignty!
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s mastery of the divine eye?

If a bodhisattva’s faculty of sight is not obstructed by walls, mountains, forests, Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, or the intermediate spaces between worlds, this is called mastery of the divine eye."
By means of this unimpeded faculty of the eye, the bodhisattva sees the immeasurable, incalculable Buddha-fields of the ten directions as a single Buddha-field.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of emptiness has no differentiation; yet, although these various Buddha-fields are distinct from one another, they neither merge nor diverge.
Furthermore, one sees all Buddhas surrounded by great assemblies as being each a single Buddha, because the characteristic of the indestructible nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such.

Because one sees the purity of a single Buddha, one sees the purity of all Buddhas; because one sees the purity of all Buddhas, one sees the purity of one's own body; because one's own body is pure, one sees the purity of all phenomena. Within this purity of one's own body and all other purities, one does not give rise to dualistic marks.

Furthermore, one sees that the disciples of the Buddhas do not differ from the purity of the Buddha; for the Bodhisattva, by seeing the disciples with right view, sees the Buddha, and by seeing the Buddha with right view, sees the disciples.

Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings throughout the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions—whether in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, among humans, or among devas, excluding those in the formless realm—the Bodhisattva, by means of the divine eye, is able to see entirely where they go in birth and death and the good or evil places they inhabit; moreover, he knows the karmic actions and their retributions of these sentient beings.
Although a bodhisattva perceives sentient beings, they do not grasp at the mark of a sentient being.
Why is this? Because they have faith in the limit of non-self.
Although they perceive actions and their retributions, they know that all phenomena are without action and without retribution.

By means of this divine eye, the bodhisattva perceives all forms as being devoid of the characteristic of form; because they have faith that all phenomena are non-existent, they know that all shapes and colors are entirely illusory, for they are fundamentally unarisen. This is called the bodhisattva’s divine eye.

Because the Bodhisattva has attained this power of the divine eye’s wisdom, he perceives according to his capacity: sometimes he sees finite forms, sometimes he sees infinite forms, and there is nothing he does not see. Although the Bodhisattva is amidst hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of sentient beings, he is able to enter into dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, until he no longer perceives even a single sentient being.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has realized that all phenomena are without self and are suchness.

This bodhisattva manifests his own body before the pure and wondrous forms of the gods in the realm of form so that the sons of the gods may see him, and yet this bodhisattva also sees the bodies of those gods.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva can cause the devas to see his own body while the devas do not see their own bodies;
or he can cause the devas to see their own bodies while they do not see the bodhisattva’s body.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
This is called the bodhisattva’s mastery of the divine eye.
Lord of Sovereignty!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mastery of the divine ear?

If a bodhisattva attains this divine ear, they hear all sounds throughout the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions—including the voices of devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all of which they hear completely.
When hearing these sounds, one makes no conceptual distinctions among them, for one has faith that all sounds possess the characteristic of being ineffable.

Furthermore, upon hearing these sounds, one does not give rise to the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of sound itself; one realizes that all sounds are fundamentally ineffable by nature and understands with faith that these sounds have no time of abiding.

Because the nature of the bodhisattva’s ear and the nature of auditory consciousness are without obstruction, when they hear these sounds and understand their true meaning, they realize that all sounds are inexpressible, for they are of the nature of cessation.
By means of this true meaning, one relies on the meaning and not on the sound, because all dharmas possess the characteristic of non-arising.

Furthermore, one hears the teachings expounded by the present Buddhas of the ten directions—immeasurable and incalculable in number—without obstruction; as heard, one is able to retain them, and having retained them, one does not forget.
Why is this? Because there is not even a single phrase that a bodhisattva does not understand before they pass away.

Regarding any Dharma they inquire about—whether it be with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, worldly or supramundane, wholesome or unwholesome, faulty or faultless, the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the Buddhas—they are able to cause these dharmas to enter into a single flavor, namely, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Thus, although they have questions, they do not cling to the six sense objects; and although they hear the Dharma, they do not dwell upon any signs (*nimitta*).
The Bodhisattva values the Dharma; he relies on the Dharma and does not rely on what is not the Dharma.
What is the Dharma? The Dharma is called freedom from defilement;

the Dharma is called signlessness; the Dharma is called the unconditioned; the Dharma is called having no place of refuge; the Dharma is called non-arising, non-origination, and non-attainment; the Dharma is called incomparable. Within this Dharma, to differentiate by means of signs, or to engage in the conceptual proliferation of grasping and rejecting, is called "what is not the Dharma."
“Vasavartin! A bodhisattva relies on the meaning and not on the words; without departing from the words, they enter into the mind that apprehends the meaning while listening to the Dharma.
What is meant by ‘entering the mind that apprehends the meaning’?

Not falling into views regarding the meaning of emptiness, views regarding the meaning of signlessness, or views regarding the meaning of wishlessness—this is called the mind that enters into the meaning.

When a bodhisattva listens to the Dharma with this mind that enters into the meaning, they rely upon the meaning; yet this meaning is unapprehendable, and even that unapprehendability is unapprehendable.
Furthermore, Sovereign King!
If a bodhisattva can listen to the teachings of all Buddhas in this way, relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not relying on sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
As for sūtras of definitive meaning, all sūtras whatsoever are of definitive meaning.
Because they rely on the meaning and because all phenomena are inexpressible, a bodhisattva is said to rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
If a person cannot thus rely on the meaning regarding any sūtra, that is called sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
Why is it called "not understanding"?
It is because these people do not understand the meaning; thus, they practice the path of defilement and are constantly led astray.
By whom are they led?
They are led astray by the literal sound of the words.
Those who understand the definitive meaning do not follow the literal sound. Why is this?
Because its meaning cannot be expressed in words, the Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are free from extremes and lack definitive characteristics.
Sovereign King!
For one who relies on the Dharma according to this principle, all sūtras are of definitive meaning; for one who does not rely on it in this way, all sūtras are of non-definitive meaning.
Furthermore, Sovereign King!
When a bodhisattva listens to and receives the Dharma from the Buddhas, they rely on wisdom and do not rely on consciousness. Why is this?

A bodhisattva knows that consciousness is false and illusory, devoid of characteristics, lacking intrinsic nature, formless, shapeless, non-resistant, and unidentifiable; knowing the characteristics of consciousness in this way is called wisdom (*jñāna*), not consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because the Bodhisattva relies on wisdom, he does not follow consciousness; knowing that the consciousness of others is likewise not consciousness, he does not cling to it. Since the nature of consciousness is such, the nature of wisdom is said to be such.
Sovereign King!
Relying on wisdom, the Bodhisattva does not abide in consciousness; thus, being able to understand what others say, he preaches the Dharma for them.
Furthermore, Sovereign King!
When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, although he uses the names of sentient beings, he relies upon the Dharma and does not rely upon sentient beings.
Why is this? If there were truly any sentient beings within my Dharma, they would never attain purity or liberation.
Therefore, Sovereign King!

All phenomena are ultimately without self and without sentient beings; it is only because of worldly conventions that the Tathāgata speaks of the existence of sentient beings. In reality, all phenomena are devoid of sentient beings; therefore, a bodhisattva relies on the Dharma and does not rely on sentient beings.

"Dharma" has the meaning of "dharmatā"; "dharmatā" has the meaning of "the nature of non-arising"; "non-arising" has the meaning of "ultimately neither arising nor acting"; and "meaning" has the meaning of "that which is ineffable."
Why is this? Because one preaches the Dharma by means of words, yet the Dharma does not reside within the words.
Therefore, while meaning is indicated through words, that which is indicated and spoken is in fact neither word nor speech.
That which involves conceptual discrimination and verbal expression is not the Buddha-dharma;
that which is without discrimination and without verbal expression is the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, it is said that non-explanation is the Buddha-dharma.
If a person wishes to enter the Buddha-dharma, they should enter it in this way, yet they should address sentient beings through speech.
When teaching the Dharma, one should not give rise to views.
If there is duality, it is not called the Buddha’s word; that which is non-dual and without discrimination is the Buddha’s word.

If there is vocal sound, it is not the Buddha-dharma; if there is discursive exposition, it is also not the Buddha-dharma. Where there is neither vocal sound nor discursive exposition, this is called the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, Sovereign King!

If a bodhisattva enters into the Buddha-dharma, they will obtain such a divine ear; by means of all sounds, they practice in accordance with the true mark of all dharmas and are able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
This is called the bodhisattva’s mastery of the divine ear.
Lord of Sovereignty!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mastery of the knowledge of others’ minds?

If a bodhisattva attains mastery of the knowledge of others’ minds, they know the minds of others through their own mind. Wherever they go to preach the Dharma to the assembly, they first observe the minds of the listeners; knowing what profound intentions these sentient beings possess, what practices, what causes, and what characteristics they follow, they preach accordingly.
Because the Bodhisattva’s own mind is pure, he enters into the purity of the minds of all sentient beings.
Sovereign King!

It is like a bright mirror reflecting various forms and colors—whether their features are long or short, large or small, coarse or fine—their images appear exactly according to their original forms. The mirror neither increases nor decreases them; it has no discrimination, yet because it is clear and pure, it is able to manifest all these images.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: because they illuminate the dharma-nature with the purity of their own mind, they are able to know all the mental states and mental factors arising in sentient beings without any obstruction.
If there are those among the assembly who possess many desires, he is able to know their minds and also perceives the signs of freedom from desire.
Why is this? Because the nature of the mind is not defiled.
If within the assembly there are those with much anger and much delusion, one who is able to know their minds will also see the signs of being free from anger and free from delusion.
Why is this? Because the nature of the mind is neither anger nor delusion.
If among the assembly there are those who delight in the Śrāvaka vehicle, he knows that the nature of the dharma through which they practice their path does not become small;
if among the assembly there are those who delight in the Pratyekabuddha path, he knows that the nature of the dharma through which they practice their path does not become middling;
if among the assembly there are those who delight in the Mahāyāna, he knows that the nature of the dharma through which they practice their path does not become great.

The Bodhisattva, in accordance with his knowledge of the nature of the minds of sentient beings, preaches the Dharma for them; yet he does not grasp at the characteristics of the mind. Although he knows the various vehicles, he preaches the Dharma without destroying the dharma-nature; because he does not destroy the dharma-nature, he does not destroy any nature, and thus he knows the conduct of sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva observes the minds of others with his own mind; his own mind and the minds of others are neither in conflict nor in conformity. He also knows the continuous arising of the mental states of sentient beings, and further understands that the nature of the mind is itself the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
"Lord of Sovereignty!
This is called the bodhisattva’s mastery of the knowledge of others' minds; by virtue of this mastery, there is nothing among gods or humans that he does not know."
"Lord of Sovereignty!
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mastery of the knowledge of past lives?

If a bodhisattva attains mastery over the knowledge of past lives, because of the strength of their power of mindfulness and the sharpness of their faculty of concentration, they recollect the events of incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas regarding their own and others' births, and explain them to others, saying: 'In that place, I was of such a kind, with such a name, surname, and lifespan, and experienced such suffering and pleasure.'"

Furthermore, he knows the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings in past lives—those with the power of causes and those with the power of conditions—and discerns that this person has the cause for the śrāvaka vehicle, this person has the cause for the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and this person has the cause for the Mahāyāna. Knowing the causes from their previous lives, he thus preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each.

Because the Bodhisattva has attained this knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajñāna*), he knows his own previous births and the various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) he planted in the presence of Buddhas. If there were roots of goodness in former lives that were not previously dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he should now dedicate those roots of goodness toward it.

Although the bodhisattva knows past lives, he also knows that the dharmas of previous existences have no coming; he does not see dharmas passing from a previous life to a subsequent life, nor does he see them passing from the present life to a previous life. He knows that all dharmas come from nowhere and go nowhere.

Furthermore, when recollecting the past, one does not give rise to views regarding the beginning, nor does one give rise to views regarding the end, the middle, or extreme views; one knows that all phenomena are without end and without middle.

Although the Bodhisattva recollects the past lives of sentient beings, they also know that the form of the past is devoid of marks; they know that the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of the past are devoid of marks. That the five aggregates of the past are devoid of marks is identical to the five aggregates of the future being devoid of marks, and that the future is devoid of marks is identical to the present being devoid of marks.

The Bodhisattva knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty regarding the past, knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty regarding the present, and knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty regarding the future.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
When a bodhisattva thus knows their past lives, their roots of goodness increase and the karmic conditions of their offenses from previous lifetimes are completely extinguished.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva realizes that the characteristics of all phenomena are neither new nor old; having attained such wisdom, they believe and understand that all conditioned phenomena are empty, like dreams.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
Just as one sees the suffering and pleasure of birth and death within a dream, so too does a bodhisattva believe and understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

One who believes and understands in this way does not grow weary in mind while coming and going through birth and death; they give rise to compassion among sentient beings and perceive all phenomena as having the characteristic of being merely provisional constructs."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Just as my coming and going through birth and death over many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas are all empty, false, and non-existent, so it is with all sentient beings; their coming and going through birth and death is false and unreal. Truly speaking, the four great elements do not arise; these four great elements are false dharmas."
"O Sovereign King!
When a bodhisattva perceives past lives, they see that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely false and illusory. Why is this?"
The Bodhisattva contemplates that the pleasures of the universal monarchs (cakravartin) of past lives all possess the characteristics of impermanence and change;
he contemplates that the pleasures of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, likewise all possess the characteristics of impermanence and change.

He also beheld the adorned and pure worlds of the various Buddhas, the adorned and pure assemblies of śrāvakas, the adorned and pure assemblies of bodhisattvas, and the adorned and pure objects they employ; he further reflected that the physical bodies of the Buddhas, though fully endowed, turn the wheel of Dharma while manifesting the characteristics of impermanence and transformation.
When reflecting in this way, one feels no attachment or regret for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva forms this thought:
"Thus, even the physical bodies of the Buddhas in these pure lands are impermanent and subject to extinction; how much more so that which I am attached to?
Thereupon, he entered into the dharma of non-self and non-belonging-to-self.
Based on the characteristic of impermanence and transformation, one should form this thought:
"All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent, yet sentient beings give rise to the notion of permanence regarding them."
He immediately gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and conceives the thought of relinquishment toward all phenomena.
Sovereign King!
This is called the bodhisattva’s mastery of the knowledge of past lives.

When a bodhisattva attains this mastery, they believe that all phenomena are impermanent; yet, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, they take on a body. They take it because it is not to be grasped, and they grasp it because it is not to be seized—doing so solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
"Vasavartin! What is called the mastery of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

If a bodhisattva, because of mastery over the mind, gives rise from the marks of the noble ones to the power of desire, the power of effort, the power of exertion, and the power of resolute conviction regarding the bases of psychic power, that bodhisattva attains this resolute conviction in the bases of psychic power. It is neither created nor produced; yet if he wishes to reach worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he can reach them all in a single thought-moment. All those sentient beings see him coming, yet he himself does not move from his original place. They see him preaching the Dharma there, while here he continues to preach the Dharma without interruption. Vasavartin!"
This is called the bodhisattva’s mastery of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

By means of this power of mastery over the bases of psychic power, if there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the bases of psychic power, the bodhisattva delivers them by means of the bases of psychic power.

If there are devas and humans who are attached to the mark of permanence, he shows them the conflagration at the end of the kalpa; these sentient beings see the trichiliocosm being entirely consumed by flames, yet this world suffers no loss or diminution.

If there are sentient beings who are arrogant and conceited, he then manifests as a Vajrapāṇi deity, brandishing a flaming vajra to show them, causing them to feel dread so that they may eliminate their arrogance and return to him in prostration and reverence.
If there are sentient beings who delight in the form of a wheel-turning monarch, he preaches the Dharma to them in the body of a wheel-turning monarch;
if there are sentient beings who delight in the form of Śakra Devānām Indra, he preaches the Dharma to them in the body of Śakra Devānām Indra;
if there are sentient beings who delight in the form of Brahmā Devānām Indra, he preaches the Dharma to them in the body of Brahmā Devānām Indra.
If there are sentient beings who delight in the form of a Māra king, he preaches the Dharma to them in the body of a Māra king;
if there are sentient beings who delight in seeing the body of a Buddha, he then manifests the body of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma to them;
or the Bodhisattva may dwell in mid-air for the sake of sentient beings, sitting cross-legged and emitting light from his body as he preaches the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who delight in adorning and purifying worlds, he then adorns the trichiliocosm, suspending silk streamers, banners, and canopies, erecting various standards and pennants, and covering everything above with jeweled nets; he burns famous incenses and performs various musical performances before preaching the Dharma.

Or, for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests the trichiliocosm as a single sea of water, covered everywhere with blue, red, crimson, and white lotuses of various kinds; within those waters he manifests a lion throne, sits upon it, and preaches the Dharma.
Or, for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests his own body sitting atop Mount Sumeru and preaching the Dharma, the sound of which reaches the Brahma Heaven.
For some sentient beings, he does not manifest his physical body, but preaches the Dharma solely through his voice;
for some sentient beings, he manifests the body of a gandharva and preaches the Dharma with the sounds of various musical instruments;
for some sentient beings, he manifests the body of a nāga king, raising clouds and thunder while emitting great flashes of lightning, and pouring down heavy rain as he preaches the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, he provides them with celestial food so that their bodies may be fully satisfied; having endowed them with complete joy and bliss, he preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are sentient beings in the hells tormented by suffering and affliction, he uses his supernormal powers to extinguish the fires of hell and, through celestial vital energy, causes every pore of their bodies to attain peace and happiness, while preaching the Dharma for them.
If there are those who are blind, he uses his power of mastery over objects at will to grant them the divine eye, causing them to regain sight, and then preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are those who are deaf, by means of his supernormal power he grants them the faculty of hearing so that they may hear sounds as he preaches the Dharma for them;
if there are those with various kinds of illnesses, he himself uses his supernormal power to cause them to be healed and then preaches the Dharma for them;

if there are those who have committed crimes and are being led to the place of execution, he uses his supernormal power to manifest a person in their stead, enabling them to escape punishment and attain peace of mind as he preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are sentient beings whose feet have been severed, hands cut off, ears and noses sliced away, or whose bodies are mutilated and hideous, who constantly feel ashamed and their spirits are despondent, I use my power of sovereign will to restore them all to wholeness and then preach the Dharma for them.

If there are sentient beings within the womb, dwelling in the impure place of stored blood, excrement, and urine, I use my power of sovereign will to transform it into a precious pavilion and multi-storied tower so they may dwell therein; once they have attained consciousness, I likewise preach the Dharma for them.

If they have just been born and their sense faculties are not yet developed, I use my power of sovereign will to make them complete, enabling them to receive and understand the teaching, and then I preach the Dharma for them.
"Vasavartin! This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the bases of psychic power; by means of such various inconceivable supernormal powers, they preach the Dharma."

By virtue of the Bodhisattva’s power of sovereign spiritual mastery (*ṛddhi*), in order to deliver those beings who worship the sun and moon, he places the trichiliocosm upon his right palm and hurls it far away to immeasurable worlds in other directions, such that all the people see it depart while this world remains unmoved in its original place;

furthermore, he takes worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and, inserting them into a single pore, raises them up to the Brahma Heaven and casts them into immeasurable worlds in other directions, yet causes all sentient beings to have no perception of coming or going;
and if worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were consumed by the fires at the end of an eon, he could extinguish them with a single breath.
Or, with both hands, they may shield the sun and moon, while their own bodies emit radiance that illuminates all worlds as they preach the Dharma.
"Lord of Sovereignty!

Such a bodhisattva may sit before the various Buddhas; if they wish to make an offering to a Buddha, they take a handful of flowers as large as Mount Sumeru and scatter them over the Buddha’s body. The flowers reach halfway up his body, and furthermore, all the grasses and trees throughout the trichiliocosm become torches, filling the world as the flames fall like rain."
"Lord of Sovereignty!

This bodhisattva manifests for all sentient beings whatever forms and colors they hold in esteem—whether the form of Śakra, Brahmā, or a śrāvaka, or the form of a pratyekabuddha. This is called the sovereign mastery of a bodhisattva’s supernormal powers."
That is to say: because one sees without obstruction through the divine eye;
because one hears without hindrance through the divine ear;
and because one attains the knowledge of others' minds, penetrating all minds and mental factors.
He realizes the knowledge of past lives because he recollects immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of the past;
he attains the bases of psychic power because he manifests all forms and colors according to his will.
“Lord of Sovereignty!

One who possesses mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can manifest all Buddha-activities for the sake of sentient beings; they can also thoroughly understand and discern the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings. Because they can deliver sentient beings by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna, they are well-known among the masses within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
because they bring sentient beings to fulfillment, they are well-known among the masses.”
They are known by the multitude because they have left the household life to practice the Path within the wholesome dharmas;
they are known by the multitude because of their power of skillful means;
they are known by the multitude because of their dedication of the *dānapāramitā*.
Because they dedicate the *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*, they are known by all;
because they subdue all Māras and cause them to plant roots of goodness, they are called "Masters of Supernatural Powers."
"Furthermore, Sovereign King!

Because a bodhisattva attains this mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vaśitā*), their physical body’s strength, renown and praise, family lineage and wealth, and retinue of followers all become universally preeminent and well-known to the multitude; for this reason, it is called 'mastery of supernormal powers. "
Furthermore, Sovereign King!

Because the bodhisattva has attained this mastery of supernormal powers, he is known by all; that is to say, he is known by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, and the Buddhas, the Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones. For this reason, he is called "widely known."
“Vasavartin! By means of these supernormal powers, the bodhisattva does not retreat from their original vow, yet is able to manifest all manner of phenomena. Vasavartin!”
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mastery over wisdom?
It refers to the wisdom of the aggregates, the wisdom of the elements, the wisdom of the sense bases, the wisdom of causes and conditions, and the wisdom of the truths.
Sovereign King!
What is meant by knowledge of the aggregates?
Form is empty of the past limit, empty of the future limit, and empty of the middle;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the past limit, empty of the future limit, and empty of the middle.
That the five aggregates are ultimately empty is called the knowledge of the aggregates.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
What is meant by the knowledge of nature?"
The nature of earth is the dharma-nature; the nature of water is the dharma-nature; the nature of fire is the dharma-nature; the nature of wind is the dharma-nature. Why is this?
Because these four natures enter into the dharma-nature and become a single nature, which is called the nature of emptiness.

Emptiness and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are identical in their lack of intrinsic existence; herein there is no earth-nature, no water-nature, no fire-nature, and no wind-nature. Why is this so?

The nature of non-disintegration is the dharma-nature; the nature of non-duality is the dharma-nature; the nature of non-arising is the dharma-nature; the nature of stainlessness is the dharma-nature; the nature of non-purity is the dharma-nature.
As it is with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), so it is with the nature of life-span, the nature of sentient beings, the nature of birth and death, and the nature of nirvāṇa.

As it is with the nature of nirvāṇa, so it is with the nature of desire, the nature of form, the nature of the formless, the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Such knowledge of these natures is not obtained through another; this is called the knowledge of natures (*dharmatājñāna*).
"Lord of Sovereignty!
What is meant by 'entering into wisdom'?
The eye, from the very beginning, is neither born nor arisen, and has no agent; [the same applies to the other sense organs]."
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind have from the very beginning been neither born nor arisen, and there is no agent.
Sovereign King!
The eye has no master; within it, there is no seer.
The ear has no master; within it, there is no hearer.
The nose has no master; within it, there is no smeller.
The tongue has no master; within it, there is no taster.
The body has no master; within it there is no experiencer.
The mind has no master; within it there is no cognizer.
Sovereign King!

The nature of the eye cannot see forms; the nature of the ear cannot hear sounds; the nature of the nose cannot smell odors; the nature of the tongue cannot know tastes; the nature of the body cannot perceive tangibles; and the nature of the mind cannot cognize phenomena.
Why is this? The eye performs no action; it is no different from grass, trees, earth, or stone.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind likewise perform no action; they are no different from grass, trees, earth, or stone.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
The eye is neither defiled nor detached; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither defiled nor detached. Why is this?"
The eye has been free from characteristics from the very beginning; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have likewise been free from characteristics from the very beginning.
Sovereign King!
If one can thus know all sense-bases (*āyatana*), one is able to leave desire behind; this is called the wisdom of entry.
"Lord of Sovereignty!

When a bodhisattva thus knows that the nature of the aggregates (skandhas) and the sense-bases (āyatanas) is neither born nor arisen, because they are ultimately extinguished; and though, having been extinguished, they undergo birth and passing away, and although they experience the nature of the aggregates and sense-bases, they do not abandon the wisdom regarding the nature of the aggregates and sense-bases—this is called mastery over wisdom."

It means knowing the nature of the aggregates and the sense bases, knowing the characteristics of the aggregates and the sense bases, yet being able not to abandon them; manifesting within the triple world while not dwelling in any fetters; and demonstrating birth and death while neither arising nor ceasing—this is called mastery over wisdom.
“Vasavartin! What is meant by ‘knowledge of conditions’?
Ignorance conditions volitional formations; yet ignorance does not form the thought: ‘I am giving rise to volitional formations.’”
Volitional formations condition consciousness, yet volitional formations do not form the thought, "I give rise to consciousness.
Consciousness conditions name-and-form, yet consciousness does not form the thought, "I give rise to name-and-form.
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, yet name-and-form does not form the thought, "I give rise to the six sense bases."
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; yet the six sense bases do not form the thought, "I give rise to contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises; yet contact does not form the thought, "I give rise to feeling.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; yet feeling does not form the thought, "I give rise to craving."
Craving conditions grasping, yet craving does not form the thought, "I give rise to grasping.
Grasping conditions becoming, yet grasping does not form the thought, "I give rise to becoming.
Becoming conditions birth, yet becoming does not form the thought, "I give rise to birth."
Birth is the condition for old age and death, yet birth does not form the thought: "I am giving rise to old age and death.
Old age and death are the conditions for sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, yet old age and death do not form the thought: "I am giving rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair."
"Lord of Sovereignty!
If a bodhisattva can contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in this way, they will not fall into any views, whether the view of annihilationism or the view of eternalism.
The bodhisattva forms this thought:"
"The dharmas belong to various conditions; when one seeks these various conditions, they cannot be found.
Thus, one attains true wisdom regarding the twelve links of dependent origination.
What is meant by "true wisdom"?

To know that the dharmas of dependent origination are identical to non-arising; that non-arising is identical to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and that emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are identical to the dharmas born of various conditions—such as the Tathāgata employs to equally attain all dharmas—is for these dharmas to be identical to the dharmas of dependent origination.

In the dharma of dependent origination, there is no arising of dharmas; therefore, it is said that one should see dependent origination as non-arising. The wisdom of the non-arising of the twelve links of dependent origination is itself the wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Vasavartin! Clarity and ignorance are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Action and non-action are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination."
Consciousness is not consciousness; these two are non-dual. One who knows this knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Name-and-form is not name-and-form; these two are non-dual. One who knows this knows the dharma of dependent origination.
The six sense bases are not the six sense bases; these two are non-dual. One who knows this knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Contact and non-contact are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Feeling and non-feeling are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Craving and non-craving are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Grasping and non-grasping are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Existence and non-existence are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Arising and non-arising are non-dual; he who knows them thus knows the dharma of dependent origination.
Old age and death are not old age and death; they are non-dual. One who knows this knows the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

That which arises from conditions has no fixed location; that which arises from conditions is selfless (*anātman*) and empty (*śūnya*). That which arises from conditions neither comes nor goes; that which arises from conditions is not real; that which arises from conditions has no single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*); that which arises from conditions has no course of action. To know it thus is called the wisdom of dependent origination.

One who sees the dharma of conditions does not see ignorance, does not see volitional formations, does not see consciousness, does not see name-and-form, does not see the six sense bases, does not see contact, does not see feeling, does not see craving, does not see clinging, does not see existence, does not see birth, and does not see aging and death. If one does not see such dharmas in this way, it is called seeing the dharma of dependent origination; if one sees the dharma of dependent origination, it is called seeing the Dharma.
What is the seeing of phenomena?
It is the seeing of phenomena that are free from passion.
What is freedom from passion?
Because the practitioner is free from defiled views regarding all phenomena, they are said to be "free from defilement"; therefore, it is said that they see the dharma of freedom from defilement.
What is meant by seeing in a way that neither increases nor decreases?
Seeing suchness in this way, one is neither moved nor attached;
seeing suchness in this way, one does not destroy the dharma-nature, nor does one perceive any conjunction.

Since suchness and the dharma-nature are neither destroyed nor conjoined, he who sees thus does not subvert the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). He who sees thus also does not see; it is not seen with the fleshly eye, nor with the divine eye, nor with the wisdom eye.

Why is this? Because the fleshly eye lacks non-action, it does not see; because the divine eye possesses the characteristic of active arising, it does not see unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); and because the wisdom-eye lacks the characteristic of conceptual discrimination, it does not see due to its non-discriminative nature.
"Vasavartin! If a bodhisattva can see all dharmas in this way, they are able to see the Buddha.

They do not see him by means of form; they do not see him by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not see him by means of the various marks; they do not see him by means of dharmas; they do not see him by means of precepts; they do not see him by means of concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation; they do not see him by means of the past; they do not see him by means of the future or the present. To see in this manner is called seeing the Buddha."
The Bodhisattva Vaśavartin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is there any object of focus such that, when a bodhisattva perceives all these dharmas in this way, they are able to see the Buddha?"
The Buddha said: "There is.
For what reason?"
Form is the characteristic of exhaustion, because its nature is non-arising; to be able to see form in this way is called seeing the Tathāgata.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characteristics of exhaustion, because their nature is non-arising; to be able to see consciousness in this way is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Precepts are unconditioned, uncreated, and unarisen characteristics; to be able to see the precepts in this way is called seeing the Tathāgata.
The same applies to concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; this is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Sovereign King!

When I was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past, I attained the vision of the Buddha’s purity. At that time, because I saw the dharma of dependent origination, I saw the Dharma; because I saw the Dharma, I saw the Tathāgata.
The Sovereign King asked:
"Prior to the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, how did you perceive the various Buddhas?
The Buddha said:
"You see by means of seeing the marks of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), but you do not see by means of seeing the non-dual dharma-body (*advaya-dharmakāya*).
Now I shall explain this for you:
from the moment I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have never seen a Buddha."
Why is this? Because one does not see by means of physical marks, it is called "seeing the Buddha.
Therefore, Sovereign King!
If a bodhisattva wishes to see the Buddha, they should do so as I saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha, because all dharmas have a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
What is this single characteristic?
It is that my own body and the body of Dīpaṃkara Buddha are likewise, and the body of Dīpaṃkara Buddha is likewise [to mine], because they are one and the same body.

To enter the single characteristic of phenomena by means of non-duality and non-distinction is called seeing the dharma of dependent origination; to see the dharma of dependent origination is called seeing the Dharma; and because one sees the Dharma, it is called seeing the Buddha.

If a bodhisattva is able, within every moment of thought, to realize cessation without it being a real cessation, and to manifest birth and death through the wisdom of skillful means such that they are not apprehended, this is called the bodhisattva’s mastery over wisdom.
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King, Volume One;
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King, Volume Two.
Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
"Vasavartin! What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowledge of the truths?

Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas realize liberation as a śrāvaka through the realization of the dharmas of the truths; yet, when a bodhisattva attains these truths without realizing [final] liberation, this is called mastery."

Those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha realize liberation as a pratyekabuddha through the realization of the Dharma of truth; yet the bodhisattva attains this truth without realizing liberation—this is called mastery.
Regarding the knowledge of the truths (*satyajñāna*): it is the knowing and seeing that the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is illusory.
How is it known and seen?

Suffering is illusory and unreal; it is suffering because it is obtained [only] through conditions, and it exists because of inversion (*viparyāsa*). If a bodhisattva knows that suffering is without birth and without arising, this is called "knowing and seeing the truth of suffering."
How is the origin [of suffering] abandoned?
All phenomena are abandoned in accordance with their origin. What is the origin?
Because origination (*samudaya*) is equal, cessation (*nirodha*) is likewise.
Because there is nowhere from which it comes, there is origination; because there is nowhere to which it goes, there is cessation. This is called the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Within this, there is no real dharma; that which has arisen must be ceased. Origination exists due to the influence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); if one ceases craving and latent tendencies, this is called the cessation of origination.
What is the truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is called the cessation of suffering because it is the ultimate extinction of the accumulation of suffering, such that there is no dharma to be destroyed.
Because all conditions and marks have ceased, all dharmas possess this mark of cessation; herein, non-arising and non-ceasing is termed the truth of cessation.
What is the truth of the path?

It is that by means of whatever path one seeks all phenomena and does not find them—whether they be wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—this is called the truth of the path.
This path is equanimous, for it does not differentiate among any phenomena;
this path is quiescent, for it is free from the fever of all fetters;
this path is peaceful and blissful, for it is free from all sorrow and affliction.
This path is untainted, for all taints have been exhausted;
this path cannot be traversed by those who grasp at anything attainable, for it is easily practiced by those who correctly cultivate meditative concentration;
this path is never abandoned by the Buddhas.
This path is signless, because it severs all signs;
because such a path does not fall into duality, it is called the Truth of the Path.
If a bodhisattva understands the Four Truths through such a gateway, this is called the knowledge of the truths (*satyajñāna*).

If a bodhisattva first teaches the Four Noble Truths for the sake of those seeking the vehicles of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, yet remains without attachment even toward these vehicles, this is called mastery over the knowledge of the truths.
Furthermore, Sovereign King!

When a bodhisattva knows that the vehicle of the śrāvakas is not to be dwelled upon, knows that the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas is not to be dwelled upon, and knows that the vehicle of the buddhas is not to be dwelled upon, this is called mastery over the knowledge of truth.
"Furthermore, Sovereign King!

If one knows the minds of all sentient beings with a single mind, and knows the nature of all mentalities with the nature of a single mind, yet does not engage in dualistic activity regarding that mental wisdom, this is called mastery over wisdom."
Furthermore, there is mastery over knowledge: he perceives the past without obstruction, yet his mind does not reach the past;
he perceives the future without obstruction, yet his mind does not reach the future;
he perceives the present without obstruction, yet his mind does not reach the present.
They do not give rise to conceptual proliferation regarding the past, future, or present.
Furthermore, they possess mastery over wisdom: they know that all conditioned phenomena are subject to exhaustion and cessation, yet they do not exhaust their roots of goodness;
they know that dharmas are unarisen, yet they gather in sentient beings by means of gathering the Dharma. This is called mastery over wisdom.

Furthermore, one does not learn from others that all phenomena possess the characteristic of ultimate cessation; rather, by means of this power of wisdom, one does not personally enter cessation while teaching and transforming sentient beings—this is called mastery over wisdom.
“Vasavartin! If a bodhisattva here wishes to attain mastery over the power of mastery in wisdom, they should follow the course of wisdom and not the course of their own will.”
What is mental activity?
All mental karma is mental activity;
all cognitive karma is mental activity.
All mental karma is the activity of the mind;
all instances of attachment that give rise to various roots of goodness are the activity of the mind;
practicing giving while falling into views, maintaining precepts while falling into signs, and practicing patience while relying on a self—all these are the activity of the mind.
To think "I am a bodhisattva" is a mental activity;
to think "I have resolved for enlightenment" is also a mental activity;
to think "I do not sever the lineage of the Buddha, I do not sever the lineage of the Dharma, and I do not sever the lineage of the Saṃgha" is likewise a mental activity.
My generating the resolve for enlightenment for the sake of benefiting sentient beings is also a mental formation;
my thinking, "I shall deliver those not yet delivered, liberate those not yet liberated, settle those not yet settled, and extinguish the unextinguished," is entirely a mental formation;

my thinking, "I am a donor, I am one who upholds the precepts, I am one who practices patience, I am one who practices diligence, I am one who practices concentration, and I am one who practices wisdom," is entirely a mental formation.
"I am one who practices loving-kindness, one who practices compassion, one who practices sympathetic joy, and one who practices equanimity"—all such [notions] are mental activities.

"I am one who practices few desires and contentment, one who practices seclusion, one who practices non-mixture, one who practices the dhūta ascetic virtues, one who dwells in an araṇya, and one who practices subtle conduct"—such distinctions are all mental activities.
"I am one who practices emptiness, I am one who practices signlessness, and I am one who practices wishlessness"—such distinctions are all mental activities.
"I am one who speaks the truth, who speaks reality, and who acts according to what he says"—all such [thoughts] are mental activities.
"I have transcended all demonic deeds and am free from the four Māras; I have severed all views and attained patience"—such discriminations are all mental activities.
"I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turn the wheel of Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder"—such discriminations are all mental activities.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
What is the intellectual activity of a bodhisattva?
To act in accordance with the sphere of non-mind, non-consciousness, and non-awareness—this is called intellectual activity."
A bodhisattva constantly performs the work of wisdom and does not give rise to the work of the mind.
What is the bodhisattva’s work of wisdom?
There are two kinds of a bodhisattva’s work of wisdom.
What are the two?
First, maturing sentient beings; second, upholding the true Dharma.
What is meant by maturing sentient beings?
A bodhisattva, according to what they know, is able to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
How does one uphold the true Dharma?
If one does not grasp at any phenomena, this is called upholding the true Dharma.
If one upholds form, one does not uphold the True Dharma;
if one upholds feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one does not uphold the True Dharma;
if one upholds the sense bases or the elements, one does not uphold the True Dharma.
If one accepts wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, one is not upholding the true Dharma;
if one accepts what is sinful or non-sinful, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane dharmas, one is not upholding the true Dharma;
if one accepts the mark of giving, one is not upholding the true Dharma.
If one receives [the perfections of] morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, yet does not uphold the true Dharma, why is this?
Because the objects of perception from which they are grasped are all non-Dharma and non-virtuous; thus, it is not the upholding of the true Dharma.
Why is this? The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata is a Dharma without marks and without obstruction; if one grasps at the marks of conditions, it is not the upholding of the true Dharma.
Such wisdom within the bodhisattva’s activities is called the activity of wisdom.
To perform the work of wisdom with such wisdom, without exhausting that wisdom, is called mastery over wisdom.
"Lord of Mastery!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mastery over insight?"

The Bodhisattva attains mastery over wisdom and is able to know the explanations and phrases of all dharmas, because he has attained the power of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge: namely, the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), the unimpeded knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), and the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).
What is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning?
It is when a bodhisattva, among all forms of speech, relies on the meaning and not on the words.
"Meaning" refers to correct knowledge regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).
What is right knowledge?
It is the ineffable meaning.
This meaning exists within speech yet possesses no distinct sound; because it has been free from all characteristics since the very beginning, it is called "meaning."
One should not depart from words to rely upon meaning; the common characteristic within words is itself the meaning.
To be able to know in this way is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, to penetrate the meaning of all phenomena is also called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning.
What is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?
A bodhisattva relies on the Dharma and does not rely on what is non-Dharma.
One who relies on the Dharma does not perceive what is non-Dharma.
Why is this? Because one knows that all phenomena are devoid of characteristics and consist of nothing but names.
Furthermore, regarding the non-obstruction of phenomena, although one may preach the three vehicles, one does not destroy the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Why is this? The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is a single nature, namely, signlessness (*animitta*).

When a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma through speech, they know that speech is identical to the nature of an echo; whatever Dharma they teach, their faith and understanding are all identical to the nature of phenomena. Being unimpeded regarding both wisdom and speech, this is called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmanirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
What is the unimpeded knowledge of language?
It is knowing the languages of all devas; knowing the languages of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
and knowing the languages of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World Protectors.

Knowing whether it is a single word, two words, or many words; whether concise or detailed; whether the speech of a man, a woman, or neither man nor woman; and whether it concerns the past, the future, or the present—he employs skillful means through his verbal expressions so that others may attain understanding.
One employs pure and sublime speech oneself, yet does not disparage the words of others.
Why is this? Because one knows that all phenomena are devoid of verbal expression.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:

"I shall preach the Dharma through words so that others may attain understanding; yet this Dharma cannot be found within words, nor can words be found within the Dharma, for from the very beginning there have been no words."
"If there are words, one should not use virtuous words to speak of unwholesome dharmas.
Therefore, you should know that words can demonstrate both good and evil.
Furthermore, regarding the absence of impediment in speech (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), it means employing the very language of sentient beings to cause them to practice the Dharma.

Why is this? Because phenomena do not act upon phenomena; yet, one can thus practice all phenomena and, by means of verbal expression, explain this practice so that others may understand it—this is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
What is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)?
If a bodhisattva is able to eloquently speak upon all syllables, is able to eloquently speak with all sounds, and is able to eloquently speak with all names and terms, this is called eloquence.
What is meant by "delight"?

When a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, they delight in the Dharma, delight in reality, and delight in the Truth. To those who have faith and delight in the Sūtras, he preaches the Sūtras; to those who have faith and delight in the Geyas, Gāthās, Udānas, Itivṛttakas, Jātakas, Vaipulyas, Adbhutadharmas, Nidānas, Avadānas, Upadeśas, and Vyākaraṇas, he preaches all of them; and to those who have faith and delight in the past, he preaches the Itivṛttakas (Past Deeds).
Regarding the various faculties (indriya) that all sentient beings delight in, he preaches the Dharma according to what they find pleasing.
