To those who delight in the faculty of faith, he preaches the Dharma by means of the faculty of faith; to those who delight in the faculty of diligence, he preaches the Dharma by means of the faculty of diligence; to those who delight in the faculty of mindfulness, he preaches the Dharma by means of the faculty of mindfulness; to those who delight in the faculty of concentration, he preaches the Dharma by means of the faculty of concentration; to those who delight in the faculty of wisdom, he preaches the Dharma by means of the faculty of wisdom. In this manner, he preaches the Dharma by means of each of these faculties.

Those with a predominance of sensual desire are divided into twenty-one thousand types; the Buddha knows that there are eighty-four thousand faculties (*indriya*), and based on these faculties, the Tathāgata is able to teach with joy, and the Bodhisattva subsequently is able to teach with joy.

Those with a predominance of hatred are divided into twenty-one thousand types; the Buddha knows that there are eighty-four thousand faculties, and based on these faculties, the Tathāgata is able to teach with joy, and the Bodhisattva subsequently is able to teach with joy.

Those with a predominance of delusion are divided into twenty-one thousand types; the Buddha knows that there are eighty-four thousand faculties, and based on these faculties, the Tathāgata is able to teach with joy, and the Bodhisattva subsequently is able to teach with joy.

The *Vipāka-vibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Miscellaneous) consists of twenty-one thousand sections; the Buddha knows eighty-four thousand faculties (*indriya*), and the Tathāgata is able to joyfully expound the Dharma according to these various faculties, as is the Bodhisattva next in turn, O Sovereign King!
This is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding these, the unimpededness with respect to meaning (*artha*), phenomena (*dharma*), expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) all have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their basis; they abide in wisdom and are subsumed by wisdom. By the power of wisdom, the bodhisattva attains mastery through these four masteries as well as other masteries.
“World-Honored One!
What is the root of wisdom?
In what does it abide?”
"By what is it subsumed?
"O Sovereign King!
Wisdom has extensive learning as its basis; it abides in the state of extensive learning and is subsumed by extensive learning."
“World-Honored One!
What is the foundation of extensive learning?
In what does it abide?”
"By what is it subsumed?
"O Sovereign King!
Much learning has the spiritual friend as its root; it abides in the station of the spiritual friend and is subsumed by the spiritual friend."
“World-Honored One!
What is the root of a spiritual friend?
Where does he abide?”
"By what is it subsumed?
"O Sovereign King!
A spiritual friend takes a heart of reverence as its basis; abiding in a heart of reverence, they are subsumed by that heart of reverence."
“World-Honored One!
What is the root of a respectful mind?
In what does it abide?”
"By what is it subsumed?
"Lord of Sovereignty!
Reverence has the profound mind as its root; abiding in the profound mind, it is subsumed by the profound mind."
“World-Honored One!
What is the root of the profound mind?
In what does it abide?”
“By what is it encompassed?
“O Sovereign King!
The profound mind takes integrity as its foundation; abiding in integrity, it is encompassed by integrity.”
“World-Honored One!
What is the root of straightforwardness?
In what does it abide?”
"By what is it subsumed?
"O Sovereign King!
Sincerity and straightforwardness take great compassion as their root; they abide in great compassion and are subsumed by great compassion."
“World-Honored One!
What is the root of great compassion? Where does it abide? By what is it encompassed?
“Lord of Sovereignty!
Great compassion has sentient beings as its basis; it dwells within sentient beings and is encompassed by sentient beings.
Why is this so, Sovereign King?
A bodhisattva, in order to deliver all sentient beings, gives rise to the mind of great compassion and the mind of omniscience; this is called the bodhisattva’s mastery of wisdom (*prajñā-vaśitā*).

Furthermore, because a bodhisattva possesses mastery of wisdom, by means of a single dharma-gate, they may, for an eon or less than an eon, extensively expound all dharmas through various diverse expressions without contradicting or deviating from the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

A bodhisattva may choose not to manifest their body in order to preach the Dharma for sentient beings, or they may produce the sound of the Dharma from the pores of their skin, preaching the Dharma in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva wishes to manifest his body to preach the Dharma to sentient beings, no heterodox teachers or scholars can exhaust his depth. Furthermore, regarding the works produced by heterodox seers—
whether they be the *mantra* and incantation scriptures such as the *Atharvaveda*, or treatises on rhetoric, or the *pāṭha* [recitations],
or various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), or various gateways of knowledge (*jñānamukha*), or the sun and moon— [the bodhisattva’s mastery is unsurpassed].
The Sūtra on the Five Planets; the Sūtra on Dreams; the Sūtra on Earthquakes; the spells and incantations of the *ḍākinīs*;
the Sūtra on the Language of Crows; the Sūtra on Birds and Beasts; the Sūtra on the Entry of Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas into the Body; the Sūtra on Royal Omens;
the Sūtra on the Signs of Abundance, Prosperity, Famine, and Scarcity; and the Sūtra on Various Pastimes and Amusements.
In this way, regarding the world’s scriptures, wisdom, arts and crafts,
literature, mathematics, physical forms, music, singing and dancing, the *konghou* lute, the *zhen* zither, and the flute— along with their melodic modulations—
the Bodhisattva, upon transforming his body, naturally understands them all within his mind; by the power of his wisdom, he is able to know them all.
They are all able to manifest them and all able to comprehend them;
although the bodhisattva knows such arts and techniques, he does not afflict sentient beings, nor does he regard them as the pure and sublime path.

“Vasavartin! The Bodhisattva Prajñāvaśavartin dwells and sits together with hundreds of thousands of millions of Brahmā kings; he manifests his own body to converse and debate with them, yet he does not become attached to the radiance, virtues, or physical marks of those Brahmā kings. Nevertheless, the Brahmā kings welcome and escort the Bodhisattva, giving rise to hearts of reverence. In this way, throughout all celestial palaces, he manifests his power of mastery yet remains unattached; he gives rise only to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Relying on the dharma of non-arising and relying on the mind that seeks to deliver all sentient beings—Vasavartin!”
This is called the bodhisattva’s mastery over wisdom.
Furthermore, Sovereign King, the bodhisattva who has mastery over wisdom causes even the celestial palaces belonging to Māra to become even more sublime;
he manifests his own body as being hundreds of thousands of millions of times superior to all that belongs to Māra.

He causes all the māras to give rise to hearts of craving and attachment; by means of this, he adorns himself and shatters the arrogant minds of the māras, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and only thereafter does he preach the Dharma.
“Vasavartin! Wisdom is the universally applicable dharma of a bodhisattva. Whether it be giving, receiving, or dedicating the gift, wisdom must be applied in these instances;
whether it be personally observing the precepts, teaching others to observe the precepts, or dedicating the observance of the precepts, wisdom must likewise be applied in these instances.”
If one practices patience or teaches others to practice patience, dedicating that patience [to enlightenment], one must also apply wisdom in this regard;
if one practices diligence oneself or teaches others to practice diligence, dedicating that diligence [to enlightenment], one must also apply wisdom in this regard;
if one practices meditative concentration oneself or teaches others to practice meditative concentration, dedicating that concentration [to enlightenment], one must also apply wisdom in this regard.

Whether reading various sutras or expounding the Dharma for others, whether maintaining right mindfulness with wisdom according to what has been heard, or in all activities—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and in all formal rituals and all states of equanimity, one should always employ wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Power of Wisdom is the master of all wholesome dharmas; the Bodhisattva Superiority of Wisdom attains superior mastery over all dharmas;
the Bodhisattva Sovereignty of Wisdom is able to act with sovereignty regarding all dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Grasping the Power of Wisdom knows that the Buddha is able to repel the armies of Māra.

A bodhisattva possessing wisdom acts with sovereign ease among all phenomena without exerting effort; just as when a person shoots an arrow upward, no further force from the bow is required when the arrow returns, so too is it for the bodhisattva: by the power of wisdom, they dispatch sovereign intelligence to enter into all wholesome dharmas.

When sitting at the site of enlightenment, he attained this power of wisdom; by means of this power, he moved the worlds of the ten directions with his right hand, shattered the great armies of Māra, and attained the ten powers of a Buddha. By virtue of these ten powers, no devas or humans are able to subdue him.

“Vasavartin! These are the mastery of precepts, the mastery of supernormal powers, the mastery of knowledge, and the mastery of wisdom. If a person has not planted roots of goodness, they will be unable to hear a sūtra such as this.”
"Lord of Sovereignty!

If there are those who, upon hearing this sutra, experience joy in their hearts, you should know that such persons have attained the four kinds of mastery; by means of these masteries, they manifest the power of sovereignty."
Why is this? Sovereign King!
These various sovereignties are not possessed by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, was filled with great joy and delight; he joined his palms in reverent salutation, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, never for a moment averting his eyes.
He spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
By means of these four powers of mastery, may all sentient beings also attain these four powers of mastery."

By the Buddha’s supernormal power, he caused the Bodhisattva Sovereign King to fill his lap with various beautiful colored flowers and fragrant blossoms, which he then scattered over the Buddha and the other bodhisattvas. Those upon whom the flowers fell all became golden in color, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
In the sky, hundreds of thousands of millions of devas raised their voices in unison and exclaimed:

"If there are sentient beings who, having faith and acceptance in these four powers of mastery, resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, those sentient beings shall adorn themselves with the adornments of the Buddha."
Why is this? World-Honored One, these four masteries all follow the mind of omniscience.
If the Buddha had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how could these sentient beings have heard such inconceivable sūtras on sovereign mastery?
After the sons of the gods had offered their praise, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign King:
"I recall that in a past age, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was a seventieth Buddha named Samantaprabhāsarāja Tathāgata, who also extensively expounded these four dharmas of mastery."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Jñānacaryāpāda who also questioned the Buddha regarding this Dharma.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained these four masteries and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), while thirty-two thousand people resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Vasavartin! At that time, I first heard of these four masteries; having heard them, I received and upheld them, until the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha when I attained them in their full perfection."
Therefore, Sovereign King!

Whether in this present age or after my parinirvāṇa, if there are those who single-mindedly seek the Buddha-way and receive and uphold this sutra, you should know that such persons will swiftly attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
When this *Īśvararāja-sūtra* was being preached, thirty-two thousand devas and humans gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

To honor the Buddha, the sons of the gods performed hundreds of thousands of musical performances and rained down celestial flowers. Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, such sounds issued forth from the various musical instruments:

"If there are sentient beings who hear this *Īśvararāja-sūtra*, believe and understand it, and accept and uphold it, you should know that these people possess keen and sharp faculties, delight in the Buddha-dharma, and possess vast wisdom. They are protected by virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), have deeply planted roots of goodness, and practice the path of great compassion toward all sentient beings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha possesses the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; does the bodhisattva also possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities?”
The Buddha told King Vaśavartin:

"There is the avaivartika bodhisattva who has long practiced and cultivated the path, attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and dwells in the eighth stage, desiring to enter the ninth stage. Protected by the skillful means of the prajñā-pāramitā, such a bodhisattva is then able to fully accomplish the ten powers of a bodhisattva, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities."
"Lord of Sovereignty!
What are the ten powers of a bodhisattva?
For the sake of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), they generate a mind of profound and firm resolve."
Because they possess a mind of loving-kindness, they have the power not to abandon any sentient being;
because they do not seek any gain or honor and have renounced all worldly adornments, they possess the power of great compassion;
because they have faith in all Buddha-dharmas, are able to accomplish these dharmas, and their minds do not regress or sink, they possess the power of great diligence.

Because they practice mindfulness and settled wisdom; because they do not violate the rules of decorum; because they abide in the power of immovable concentration and remain free from the two extremes;
because they accord with the dharma of dependent origination; because they sever all views and do not engage in distinct conceptual proliferations;
because they possess the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* to bring sentient beings to completion; because they undergo immeasurable births and deaths; and because they cultivate virtuous qualities.

Because they are insatiable; because they have faith and understanding that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like dreams; because they possess the power of tirelessness within birth and death (*saṃsāra*); because they contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);
because there is no self (*ātman*), no person (*pudgala*), and no sentient being (*sattva*); because they have faith and understanding in the non-arising and non-originating nature of phenomena;
because they have faith and delight in the discourse on the non-arising of phenomena; [this is] the power of the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
Because they enter into the states of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; because they contemplate the gates of liberation;
and because they attain the understanding and insight of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they obtain the power of the gates of liberation.
Because they do not rely on the wisdom of others regarding profound dharmas; and because they contemplate the mental activities of all sentient beings, they possess the power of unimpeded wisdom.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
These are called the ten powers of a bodhisattva.
Lord of Sovereignty!"
What are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva?

Because they have attained dhāraṇī, because they are able to retain everything they hear, and because they never forget or lose mindfulness, they are fearless when preaching the Dharma in the midst of a great assembly;

because they preach the Dharma according to the faith and understanding of all sentient beings—just as one prescribes medicine according to the illness—and because they know and perceive the faculties of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma accordingly, they are fearless in the midst of a great assembly.

Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, he preaches the Dharma without any hesitation or difficulty; there is no east, south, west, or north such that someone might come to question him and he would be unable to answer. He is even free from the slightest sign of fear, freely enduring the challenges and interrogations of sentient beings, answering according to their questions without any apprehension.
Because he is well able to sever doubts, he preaches the Dharma within the great assembly without fear.
"Lord of Sovereignty!
These are called the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva.
Lord of Sovereignty!"
What are the eighteen unique qualities of a bodhisattva?
From birth, a bodhisattva is naturally able to practice giving without being instructed:
"You should practice giving; you should delight in the mind of renunciation."
If Māra were to take the form of a Buddha and come to say to him,
"If you practice giving, you will fall into hell," it would be impossible for the Bodhisattva to give rise to a mind of stinginess or regret.

Joyfully relinquishing all things and distributing them as gifts, he practices this giving for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, seeking no karmic reward but for the benefit of sentient beings; this is the first unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! A bodhisattva is naturally able to maintain the precepts without being taught by another; even though he does not encounter a Buddha, nor does he receive the precepts from others, he is well able to guard and uphold all precepts and always delights in maintaining them. This means that although he may be a householder, he is fully able to practice and uphold everything as prescribed in the precepts; if he leaves the home life, he is able to fulfill everything taught in the *Śīla-sūtra* without needing instruction. He does not abandon the precepts even for the sake of his life or various circumstances, and all the precepts he maintains accord with Bodhi. For the purpose of severing the dharma of breaking the precepts among sentient beings—this is the second unique quality of a bodhisattva.”

“Vasavartin! If poor and lowly persons, as well as *caṇḍālas* or craftsmen, should respond with anger and malice, reviling him with harsh words or dismembering his limbs one by one, the Bodhisattva at that time remains unmoved in mind. He universally moistens such sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness; though he possesses the power to retaliate, he does not inflict harm. Relying solely upon the Dharma, he endures this suffering for the sake of the Buddha-Dharma’s conditions, and he further vows that these people may attain wholesome purity and give rise to great adornment. This is the third unique quality of a Bodhisattva.”

“Vasavartin! Although a bodhisattva encounters urgent distress, they still press forward, neither slackening nor resting, never giving rise to a mind of retreat or despondency. If they see a śrāvaka enter nirvāṇa, or see the sufferings of the world, their mind does not crave or delight in the dharma of the śrāvaka’s extinction.
If they see a pratyekabuddha attain extinction, or again see the sufferings of birth and death, their mind does not crave or delight in the dharma of the pratyekabuddha’s nirvāṇa.”

If one sees that the Buddhas have already achieved great benefit and entered parinirvāṇa with the Buddha-dharma fully complete, yet perceives that one’s own body has not yet attained the fulfillment of the six pāramitās and all the Buddha-dharmas, one does not become despondent in mind regarding these dharmas but exerts oneself with diligence, thinking: "I shall attain extinction through this Mahāyāna nirvāṇa. These are the four unique qualities of a bodhisattva.
"Lord of Sovereignty!

Whether a bodhisattva becomes a wheel-turning king, Śakra, or the Māra-king, and enjoys sensual pleasures while hundreds of thousands of court ladies perform celestial music, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the immeasurable states of mind (*apramāṇa-citta*) will all manifest before him. He always delights in abandoning places of clamor and bustle; he conceives a sense of great terror toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*); he conceives a sense of great impurity toward the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*); he conceives a sense of enmity toward the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); he conceives a sense of poisonous snakes toward the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); he conceives a sense of an empty village toward the sense bases (*āyatana*); he conceives a sense of hostile thieves toward his own kinsmen; and he conceives a sense of being among corpses toward his palace, residence, and court ladies. He seeks only to practice the Dharma, seeks only to see the Buddha, and constantly contemplates how to deliver all sentient beings."

From the sounds of music, the sounds of dhyāna and dharmic resonance emerge; even when Māra occasionally obstructs these sounds, by the power of roots of goodness from previous lives, they hear in the air the voices of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. Having heard these sounds, they renounce the sovereign pleasures of the world, leave the household life, and enter the forest. This is the fifth unique quality of a bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! Within the worldly meditative concentrations, the bodhisattva does not give rise to the notion of solidity; through the discernment of wisdom, he remains free from all views, relying on the Dharma and its meaning. This uncommon quality extends even to his dreams, wherein he gives rise neither to the view of a self nor to the view of dharmas.”

The bodhisattva is not driven by the fetters or the entanglements of views; being free from doubt and regret, even Māra cannot obstruct him or cause him to doubt and regret, thereby leading him away from the true Dharma.
For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, a bodhisattva may even transgress formal rules and rituals without harboring any doubt or regret therein.
Sovereign King!
These are the six unique qualities of a bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! From the moment of birth, the bodhisattva naturally attains purity of body; he abstains from taking life, and does not cause harm or injury with hands, feet, swords, staves, tiles, or stones. He constantly relinquishes weapons; his means of livelihood are abundant and sufficient, lacking nothing. Even a single handful of grass, if not given, he does not take. Though precious jewels fill the ground, he does not give rise to a mind of greed. Even when facing hunger, poverty, or the brink of death, he does not sustain himself through wrong livelihood.”

Constantly practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) up to the level of mental conception, not dwelling on the five desires and remaining free from the afflictions of desire, not engaging in unrighteousness on account of the five desires, and taking wisdom as the foremost to accomplish wholesome bodily actions—these are the seven unique qualities of a bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! A bodhisattva purifies the karma of speech; their words are true and real, and their speech accords with practice. They do not deceive themselves, nor do they mislead the Buddhas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others.”
The Bodhisattva does not engage in divisive speech; his retinue and loved ones remain inseparable from him from beginning to end.

The Bodhisattva does not engage in harsh speech; he always practices loving speech, gentle speech, and harmonious speech—avoiding evil speech and coarse speech—and instead employs reasoned speech, speech that brings peace and happiness, speech preceded by kindness, and speech that is concordant and pleasing.

Regarding harsh speech, coarse words, and piercing, bitter language—which people find unpleasant to hear and which cause both self-affliction and affliction to others—a Bodhisattva never allows such speech to issue from their mouth.

A bodhisattva does not engage in meaningless speech; if something exists, they say it exists, and if it does not exist, they say it does not exist. Because their profound mind is pure, all their verbal karma is pure.
Sovereign King!

Because the Bodhisattva attains these unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), in every birth he is always endowed with a mouth that speaks in accordance with the Dharma. By means of such speech, he causes those who are impure to attain purity, and causes those who are already pure to give rise to a mind of reverence and service. Because of this profound mind and these unique qualities, he attains a mouth of truthful speech; whatever he says is entirely real and without falsehood. These are the eight unique qualities of a Bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! A bodhisattva possesses mastery over his own mind and attains autonomous conduct; he does not covet the property of others, does not harbor anger toward sentient beings, practices right view, and never forgets the bodhisattva’s mind—the peerless mind.”

A bodhisattva always remains free from all deceitful and crooked thoughts, constantly practicing a virtuous and pure mind of compassion day and night; this constitutes the ninth unique quality of a bodhisattva.

"Vasavartin! In whatever place a bodhisattva is born, they are the most eminent and supreme among all scriptures, incantations, medical arts, and mathematics; without requiring instruction from a teacher, they naturally understand them and fully master them. Furthermore, regarding both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, they attain wisdom that does not depend on others, nor do they rely on or seek out the words of others. They are constantly gazed upon by devas and worldly people, and all who hear their speech follow and learn from it. These are the ten unique qualities of a bodhisattva."

“Vasavartin! A bodhisattva may treat the various illnesses of sentient beings without seeking profit or sustenance, taking great compassion as his primary motive. When treating their illnesses, he makes this vow:
‘I shall cause sentient beings to attain the supramundane Dharma, extinguish all suffering and affliction, and lead them to nirvana.’”
"These are the eleven unique qualities of a bodhisattva.
'Lord of Sovereignty!
A bodhisattva does not seek nor pray for the position of a Cakravartin king, nor the station of Śakra or Brahmā, yet he naturally attains them.'"

Why is this? A bodhisattva does not practice the path for the sake of physical beauty or majesty; nor does he practice the path for the sake of worldly kin, rank, position, fame, or praise. Such merit is obtained without seeking it; this is the twelfth unique quality of a bodhisattva.
"Vasavartin! When a bodhisattva dwells in a state of noble dignity, long-lived devas who have previously seen the Buddha will constantly come to protect and support them, exhorting them thus:

'You should perform these practices; by performing these deeds, you can reach bodhi. This is a dharma of regression; this is a dharma of progress. For one who practices in this way, the faculties will accord with anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

These celestial deities constantly provide such appropriate exhortations and inspirations, ensuring that [the bodhisattva] does not deviate from or lose *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the thirteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva.

"Vasavartin! If there are violent, wrathful, and evil people who see the physical, verbal, and mental karma of this bodhisattva, they will be unable to inflict harm upon them, and their minds will attain wholesome purity."
If there should be anyone who harms this bodhisattva, they should endure it without retaliation, causing that person’s mind to become pure so that they may abide in the Dharma.
If there are sentient beings who injure the bodhisattva, [the bodhisattva] shall not cause them to fall into the evil realms because of this.
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, the Bodhisattva has already attained the fully perfected, uncommon, virtuous, and pure vow:
"If there are sentient beings who harm or afflict me with body, speech, or mind, may they not fall into the evil realms because of this."
"Because the Bodhisattva purely maintains the precepts, he attains everything according to his vows; this is the fourteenth unique quality of a Bodhisattva.
'Lord of Sovereignty!

There may be sentient beings who are stingy and greedy, lacking in faith, who do not perceive the workings of karma, do not rely upon the retribution of fruits, and do not recognize the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, their minds are neither good nor pure, and they are unable to pay respectful homage. When listening to their words, they do not show respect, nor do they conceive of them as something rare and marvelous.'"

When these sentient beings behold the conduct of this bodhisattva’s body, speech, and mind, as well as his dignified demeanor, discourse, and debate, their minds immediately become purified; they pay homage, follow his example, and give rise to a sense of reverence and wonder.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has attained the unshared dharmas; these are the fifteen unshared dharmas of a bodhisattva.
"Lord of Sovereignty!

If all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, sages, great beings, brahmins, and other world-teachers see this bodhisattva, they will conceive of him as their teacher and venerable; among these people, his name shall be the most supreme.

Furthermore, the world-teachers—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, and brahmins—approach this bodhisattva, bowing their bodies in reverent salutation, providing service and attending to his needs; even the disciples of these teachers likewise pay him homage, honor, and escort him, perceiving his superiority in their minds. Having attained such faith, this constitutes the sixteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! In whatever kingdom, village, or city a bodhisattva dwells, they are able to cultivate wholesome dharmas and abandon unwholesome dharmas; they are able to transform sentient beings and protect the True Dharma. Born therein, they attain right view. In the place where their parents gave them birth, they are always honored, revered, and respected by their teachers and elders. Within that kingdom, the lives of sentient beings do not end in falling into the evil realms.”

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings through wholesome dharmas and cause them to practice merit; consequently, after their lives end, they are all reborn among humans and devas. This is the seventeenth unique quality of a Bodhisattva.

“Vasavartin! Because a bodhisattva accords with all factors conducive to enlightenment and is fully endowed with all types of clear knowledge and supernormal powers, none of the māras can find an opportunity to harm them; this is the eighteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva.”

“Vasavartin! Why are they called the ‘unshared dharmas’? Because Bodhisattvas accord with all Buddha-dharmas, these are not possessed by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, let alone by ordinary worldlings!”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One now bestows upon all bodhisattvas the illumination of the Dharma of great wisdom and the infinite light of the Dharma."

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing this sutra, takes no pleasure in other sutras; if a person hears this sutra and receives, maintains, reads, and recites it, they have already received and maintained all the Buddha-dharma;
if a person, having received and maintained this sutra, explains it for others, they are thereby able to bring sentient beings to maturity through the True Dharma of the Buddha;
and if a person correctly practices this sutra, they are correctly practicing all the Buddha-dharma.
If a person attains patience regarding this sutra, it is called "conformable patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti);
if a person practices according to what is taught in this sutra, they are then in accord with the practice of all dharmas.
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who does not depart from this sutra, you should know that such a person has already attained all the vidyās and supernatural powers and is seated at the site of enlightenment.
The Buddha told King Vaśavartin:

"As you have said, if a person does not depart from this sutra, you should know that such a person has attained all the vidyās and supernormal powers (abhijñā) and is seated at the place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Sovereign King! "

In the past, prior to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, before the Buddhas Vīradeva, Tiṣya, Puṣya, and Prabhāsa, there was a Buddha named Devendra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

That Buddha-world is adorned, pure, abundant, and joyful, filled with devas and humans. Its land is level and even, with lapis lazuli for its ground. Jāmbūnada gold forms lotuses that cover the entire land, which are soft, supple, and smooth like celestial garments.

At that time, the physical appearance, stature, means of subsistence, gardens, groves, ponds, and pavilions of the people of the world were all like those in the Tuṣita Heaven; whatever food and drink they required arrived as soon as it was thought of, no different from that of the devas, except for the difference in names.
In that trichiliocosm, the Buddha is the Dharma King; therefore, that Buddha is titled "Heavenly King.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King sits upon his rightful throne and transforms the people through the Dharma so that none fail to obey and submit, so it is with him.
The Tathāgata Heavenly King was likewise; seated upon the lion Dharma-throne, he expounded the Dharma for all devas and humans.
The area where the great assembly sat measured eighty-four thousand yojanas from east to west, and the same distance from south to north.

When the Celestial King Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, his voice pervades the trichiliocosm; all the devas and humans pay him full respect, honor, and praise, practicing the unsurpassed Dharma as an offering of the Dharma.
The sentient beings in that land—none take pleasure in inferior teachings, but delight solely in the Buddha-dharma;
there is not even the name of śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, much less those who have resolved their minds toward such practices;
there are only bodhisattvas as their retinue.
There are no women there, nor is even the name of sexual desire heard; all are born by spontaneous transformation, sitting cross-legged upon lotus flowers, delighting only in the Three Dharmas.
What are these three?
First, delighting in seeing the Buddha;
second, delighting in hearing the Dharma.
Third, they take pleasure in contemplating the Dharma and delight in the practice of renunciation.

These multitudes of people cultivate the sutras and the Dharma, remaining ever heedful; endowed with both merit and wisdom, their lifespan lasts for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. At the end of life, they are reborn in the heavens, meaning they arrive in the lands of other Buddhas.
If there is a bodhisattva whose life is about to end, he ascends into the air to a height of seven tala trees and proclaims in a great voice:
"I shall now pass away from this land."
When the assembly of seated bodhisattvas heard these words, they all gathered together to test his patience in the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) and spoke thus:
"What kind of dharma is subject to retrogression?"
"What kind of phenomena arise?
At that time, this bodhisattva spoke these words in the midst of the great assembly:
"In this, there are no phenomena that either decline or arise; when the Tathāgata attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, he knew that all phenomena neither decline nor arise."

Why is this? Form does not regress and does not arise; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not regress and do not arise. Furthermore, there is no other distinct dharma that can be definitively found—neither a self, nor a sentient being, nor a life-span—that either regresses or arises.

When the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he realized that all dharmas are empty and signless; these empty and signless dharmas neither regress nor arise. All dharmas are beyond limits, do not constitute limits, do not give rise to limits, and are the limit of non-arising. The Buddha took this as his realization, and thus these various limits likewise neither regress nor arise.
"Retreat is defined as the separation of conditions; birth is defined as the convergence of conditions; yet these very conditions neither retreat nor are born.

After this Bodhisattva had preached this Dharma in the midst of the great assembly, he then withdrew. Once his body was extinguished, leaving no ashes and no smoke, he was immediately reborn before a presently living Buddha in another direction.

This Buddha, King of Devas, and his bodhisattvas do not wear the *kāṣāya*; they all wear naturally produced, pure, and exquisite celestial robes, and they are likewise free from fetters and delusions.

The people of that world are harmonious and compliant, having all attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They do not extensively expound the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, yet because the faculties of those beings are sharp and keen, they attain awakening with even a slight prompting.

When the Buddha Tianshou preaches the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, all the devas and humans are able to understand it universally; some attain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), some attain dhāraṇīs, some attain the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid), and some attain various samādhis.

“Vasavartin! The great fame of this Buddha, King of Devas, flows everywhere throughout the ten directions. Among all devas and humans, he extensively expounds this Sūtra on the Four Sovereign Powers, and seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Pure Light who had not yet received a prediction of enlightenment. He thought to himself:

"The predictions now being bestowed upon these bodhisattvas are not due to their observance of the precepts, their ritual practices, their cultivation of the path, their mindfulness and wisdom, their skillful means and spiritual powers, or their *dhāraṇīs* and *samādhis*, which are superior to my own. For what reason do they receive their predictions while I do not?"
At that time, the Buddha Devendra, knowing his thoughts, addressed Viśuddhaprabha, saying: "Good son!
In a future age, there shall be a Buddha who appears, named Dīpaṃkara; that Buddha shall bestow upon you the prediction of enlightenment."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Bodhisattva Pure Light was filled with great joy; ascending into the air, he spoke these words:
“If the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appears only after the passing of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you should know that I have already received the prediction of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.”
"Why is this? Because all that the Buddhas speak is free from falsehood; the Buddhas are those who speak only truth.
"O Sovereign King!"
"What do you think? Was that Bodhisattva Pure Light at that time anyone else?
It was none other than myself.
Since then, I have encountered the Buddha Radiance; from that Buddha, I heard this Dharma, and having heard it, I received and upheld it, thereby attaining the Samādhi of the Seal of Light."
After this, I again encountered the Buddha Puṣya; from that Buddha, I heard this Dharma, and having heard it, I received and upheld it, thereby attaining the Samādhi of Multitudinous Radiance.
After this, I again encountered the Buddha Tiṣya; I heard this Dharma, and having heard it, I received and upheld it, thereby attaining the Samādhi of Illumination.
After this, I again encountered the Buddha Mahātejas; from that Buddha I heard this Dharma, and having heard it, I received and upheld it, thereby attaining the *anulomikī kṣānti*.

After this, I again encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; from that Buddha I attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* and realized these four masteries, namely: mastery over precepts, mastery over supernormal powers, mastery over knowledge, and mastery over wisdom.

“Vasavartin! For this reason, whether in the present age or after my parinirvāṇa, if good sons and good daughters seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle hear this sutra and, having heard it, receive and uphold it, you should know that they shall all swiftly attain the true wisdom of bodhi, obtain these four masteries, be able to turn the wheel of Dharma, and shall obtain the light of wisdom within the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Buddha.”

When this sutra was being preached, sixteen thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and twelve thousand people all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and hundreds of thousands of millions of devas joyfully proclaimed:

"Wherever this sutra is preached, one should know that the Buddha himself is present there; if any sentient beings hear this sutra, one should know that their roots of goodness are profound and deep."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?”
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The name of this sutra is 'The Four Powers of Sovereignty'; you should receive and uphold it as such."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva Īśvararāja, along with Ānanda and all the devas and humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, received and upheld it with joy.
The Scripture of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King, Scroll II.
